# Acts 15:1–20 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## v. 1 — "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved."

- **The Judaizers arrive.** "Certain men came down from Judea" — they were not sent by the apostles but came on their own initiative. Gill notes that according to Epiphanius they may have been Cerinthus and his followers. They were "Judaizing Christians" — believers who insisted that Gentile converts must first become Jews before becoming Christians. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)
- **The teaching.** They taught that circumcision was necessary for salvation — not merely a cultural practice. Enduring Word notes this "struck at the very heart of salvation by grace through faith." They made a negative judgment on Paul and Barnabas's entire Gentile mission. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Precept Austin** calls this "an attack on *sola fide*" (faith alone). The imperfect tense ("began teaching") indicates they were persistently inculcating this error, not merely mentioning it. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary)
- **Ellicott** observes they likely claimed to speak in the name of James (though James later repudiates having authorised them, v. 24). They may have rested their case on James 2:10 about keeping the whole law. Circumcision had been an "everlasting covenant" (Gen. 17:13) and had never been formally abrogated — so their argument had apparent Old Testament force. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/15.htm) (excerpt from search results)
- **MacArthur (GTY/Baptist):** These were "self-appointed guardians of legalism" with no backing from Jerusalem. He suggests they may have followed Paul and Barnabas's missionary route, visiting every city to spread the same false teaching — which would explain why Paul wrote Galatians to combat this very heresy. [https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1](https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1)

## v. 2 — "After engaging these men in sharp debate, Paul and Barnabas were appointed… to go up to Jerusalem"

- **No small dissension.** Enduring Word notes this shows Paul and Barnabas as true shepherds who confronted and disputed with promoters of false doctrine. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Gill** explains that the church at Antioch, seeing the difference could not be settled locally, wisely resolved to send Paul, Barnabas, and others (including Titus, per Gal. 2:1) to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders. The Jerusalem church was the most ancient and several apostles resided there. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** raises the question whether the incident in Galatians 2:11 (Paul rebuking Peter at Antioch) preceded and actually caused this Council. It notes the expression "came down from Judea" strongly resembles Galatians 2:12. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/15.htm) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 3 — "Sent on their way by the church, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles"

- **Gill** explains that Phoenicia and Samaria lay between Syria and Judea, so their route naturally took them through these regions. Believers had already been established in both places (Acts 8:5; 11:19). The report of Gentile conversions "caused great joy unto all the brethren" — Gill adds that where there is true grace, there will be joy at the conversion of sinners. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)
- **Enduring Word** notes this contrasted sharply with the "certain men from Judea" who brought trouble, not joy. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)

## v. 4 — "On their arrival in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and apostles and elders"

- **Gill:** They were received kindly — "received into their houses, and accommodated with everything convenient." The apostles mentioned are particularly James, Cephas (Peter), and John, who gave Paul and Barnabas "the right hand of fellowship" (Gal. 2:9). They declared "all things that God had done with them." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)
- **Fortner (StudyLight):** Identifies Paul as "the apostle to the Gentiles" — the first spokesman at the conference before the more formal council session began. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 5 — "Some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, 'The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.'"

- **Enduring Word (Guzik/Pentecostal-charismatic):** These were Christians who had been Pharisees. For a Pharisee truly to be a Christian required more than acknowledging Jesus as Messiah — he had to forsake his attempts to justify himself by law-keeping. Guzik notes: "You can't just add Jesus and now say 'Jesus helps me to justify myself through keeping the law.'" Paul himself was a former Pharisee who came to know that Jesus was his salvation, not the way to his salvation. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Gill:** These were members of the church who still "retained many of their pharisaical tenets." They rose up in opposition as Paul and Barnabas were relating their success among Gentiles. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)
- **Guzik** suggests passages they might have quoted include Exodus 12:48-49 and Isaiah 56:6, arguing the covenant Gentiles were invited to join was a covenant of circumcision. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)

## v. 6 — "The apostles and elders met to look into this matter."

- **Enduring Word:** The leaders didn't just let the issue sit or leave it to individual conscience — the matter was too important. The question was immense: "Are Christians made right with God by faith alone, or by a combination of faith and obedience of the Law of Moses?" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **MacArthur (GTY/Baptist):** Notes the apostles and elders met privately first, then followed with a public session. He calls this the "first great council of the early church." [https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1](https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1)
- **Precept Austin (quoting MacArthur):** MacArthur calls the Jerusalem Council "the first and the most significant of all" church councils because "it fixed the most momentous doctrinal question of all: What must a person do to be saved?" The apostles and elders "affirmed for all time the truth that salvation is wholly by God's grace through faith alone, apart from any human efforts." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary)

## v. 7 — "After much discussion, Peter got up and said… God made a choice among you that the Gentiles would hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe."

- **Enduring Word:** Peter began with a history lesson, recounting God's work through him with Cornelius (Acts 10). "A good while ago" — perhaps 10–20 years earlier. Peter reminded them that God had already settled this question. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Gill:** "God made choice among us" — it pleased God in His providence to single Peter out from the rest of the apostles and, in a very extraordinary manner, call him to preach to Cornelius. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)
- **Gray's Concise Bible Commentary (StudyLight):** Notes this is Peter's last appearance in Acts, and "it is remarkable that as an apostle of the circumcision… he should have been used by the Holy Spirit to reprove the error of the Judaizing teachers." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 8 — "God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us."

- **Dunagan (StudyLight):** God knew Cornelius was a genuine believer and "gave His approval of what Peter was doing by sending the Holy Spirit upon Cornelius and his household as He had sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles in Acts chapter 2." All this was done without teaching Gentiles they had to be circumcised or keep the Law. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Gill:** "God which knoweth the hearts" — He knew with what sincerity Cornelius sent for Peter, with what earnestness they attended to his words. God bore witness by giving the Spirit "even as he did unto us" — including the extraordinary gifts (tongues), though they were uncircumcised. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)

## v. 9 — "He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith."

- **Enduring Word:** Peter's point came straight from his vision of clean and unclean animals (Acts 10:28). The Pharisees thought Gentiles were inherently "common" or "unclean" and had to be made holy by the Law. But "Christians are not only saved by faith; they are also purified by faith." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Dunagan:** Peter's choice of the word "cleansing" is deliberate because "in the back of the dispute was the question of purity, which the Pharisees insisted came through observance of the Law and circumcision." The real uncleanness of the heart is cleansed by faith, not ritual. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Gill:** This purification by faith is "the circumcision of the heart, of which the other was only typical." God alone can purify the heart; it cannot be done by ceremonial ablutions, moral works, or submission to ordinances. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)

## v. 10 — "Why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?"

- **Enduring Word:** Peter observes that the law was a yoke that Israel could never bear. From the golden calf at Sinai to Sabbath-breaking in Nehemiah's day, Israel failed under the law from beginning to end. "Those of the sect of the Pharisees who believed made a critical mistake. They looked at Israel's history under the law with eyes of nostalgia, not truth." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Schaff (StudyLight):** "To impose new obligations upon these Gentile churches… would be nothing else than tempting or trying God by demanding new proofs of His will" — since God had already shown in Cornelius's case that Gentiles who believed were full partakers of all blessings. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Gill:** "It is common with the Jews to call the law a yoke." The yoke here means not just circumcision or the ceremonial law, but the whole moral law — which circumcision obliged one to keep perfectly (Gal. 5:3). "Neither the apostles, nor their fathers, were ever able to do, nor any mere man whatever." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)

## v. 11 — "We believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are."

- **MacArthur (GTY/Baptist):** This is "Peter's view" — summarizing the private conference of apostles and elders: "We believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." MacArthur emphasizes: "How are you saved? Grace. That's the only thing you see in there… God saves purely apart from anything you ever did." [https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1](https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Peter turned the expected order around: a Jew would normally say "Gentiles can be saved by grace, just like us." But Peter said "we [Jews] shall be saved in the same manner as they [Gentiles]" — putting Jews and Gentiles on identical footing. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Schaff:** "The believing Jew, who has tried to keep the law and failed, will be saved like the Gentile through the power of the blood of Jesus." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/scn/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Dunagan:** Notes that "one is not saved by faith only and neither is one saved by grace alone" — the same plan of salvation applies to all: obedience to Jesus Christ (Jn. 14:6; Heb. 5:9). This reflects a Churches of Christ perspective that insists on baptism as part of the salvation response. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 12 — "The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles."

- **Enduring Word:** The silence shows "these men were all of an honorable heart. They were willing to listen, and to be persuaded if wrong." Barnabas and Paul simply confirmed Peter's point: God has accepted the Gentiles — shouldn't we? [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Gill:** The multitude "kept silence" upon Peter's oration, "they were all satisfied with, and by their silence acquiesced in, what Peter said." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)

## v. 13 — "When they had finished speaking, James declared, 'Brothers, listen to me!'"

- **Enduring Word:** This James was not the apostle (martyred in Acts 12:2) but "James the Just" — the half-brother of Jesus (Matt. 13:55), brother of Jude, and author of the Epistle of James. Bruce notes the church's readiness to recognize his leadership "was due more to his personal character and record than his blood relationship with the Lord." Boice notes "James was the chairman of the council, not Peter." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Fortner (StudyLight):** It was fitting that James bring the concluding message as "our Lord's half brother, pastor of the church at Jerusalem." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 14 — "Simon has told us how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people to be His own."

- **Enduring Word:** James uses a striking paradox. The Greek word for Gentiles (*ethne*) and for people (*laos*) were contrasting terms for Jews — *laos* was the people of God, never the *ethne*. James declares that God has visited the *ethne* to take from them a *laos* — "God's people includes the Gentiles." Marshall is quoted: "The paradox… is striking." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Precept Austin** notes that "Simon" is Peter's Hebrew name (Simeon), used here by James in a Semitic context. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary)

## vv. 15–17 — "The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: 'After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David… so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name.'"

- **Enduring Word:** James judged the new work of God by the way any work should be judged — by "what is written." The quote is from Amos 9:11-12, showing that Gentile inclusion had a biblical foundation. "Councils have no authority in the church unless it can be shown that their conclusions are in accord with Scripture" (Stott). The rebuilt "tabernacle of David" points to a church made of both Jew and Gentile. Crucially, the Gentiles remain Gentiles — "they were not Gentiles who had been made Jews." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Fortner:** James gave the opinion of the apostles, the Holy Spirit, and the New Testament in four points. The first: "The calling of the Gentiles in one body with the Jews was foretold by the prophets." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 18 — "that have been known for ages."

- **Dunagan (StudyLight):** "Since God had foretold a long time ago that the Gentiles would be a part of the kingdom, without circumcision, it should not be opposed and resisted by us. We rather should get our ideas in harmony with God's revealed will!" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Fortner:** "The fall of Israel and the calling of the Gentiles was according to the eternal purpose of God." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Precept Austin (quoting Grant):** "Known unto God are all His works from eternity. God was not taken by surprise." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary)

## v. 19 — "It is my judgment, therefore, that we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God."

- **Enduring Word:** "Therefore I judge" — the Greek is even stronger: "I determine" or "I resolve" (Expositor's). James spoke with authority, and the decision was presented as the mutual decision of all present (v. 25). Clarke: "The rest either argued on the subject, or gave their opinion; James alone pronounced the definitive sentence." Guzik adds: "The Protestant Reformers wisely and insistently pointed out that councils have erred and do err." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Dunagan:** "This is the only conclusion that James can reach from the facts presented. Notice how the apostles have argued. Both Peter and Paul had offered approved examples and necessary inferences and James has offered direct commands… None of this was argued on the basis of feelings, the culture, or human opinion." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Judgment" should be "sentence" — "the best word, as expressing the decisive judgment of St. James, which, being delivered with the authority of his office at the close of the debate, carried with it the suffrages of the whole council." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/15.htm) (excerpt from search results)

## v. 20 — "Abstain from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood."

- **Enduring Word (Guzik/Pentecostal-charismatic):** These were not burdensome laws but appeals to love — designed to preserve Jewish-Gentile fellowship without requiring Gentiles to become Jews. The four restrictions are understood within the "Law of Love": don't unnecessarily antagonise Jewish neighbours. On "sexual immorality" (*porneia*), Guzik argues it does not merely mean sex outside marriage (which all Christians recognised as wrong) but "the specific marriage regulations required by Leviticus 18, which prohibited marriages between most family relations" — something Jews would find offensive but Gentiles would think little of. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)
- **Pett (StudyLight):** The first two (idol-food and sexual immorality) were basic — avoidance of idolatry and maintaining godly society. The second two (strangled things and blood) were necessary for Jewish and Gentile Christians to eat together, since eating blood had been forbidden since Genesis 9:4-6. "It was not a question of salvation but of fellowship." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Gray (StudyLight):** These things were "not distinguished as Mosaic prohibitions, but based on the earlier covenant of Noah (Genesis 9:4), binding equally on Gentile and Jew." Nevertheless v. 21 indicates they were to show suitable respect for Jewish neighbours instructed in these things from the OT Scriptures. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Fortner (StudyLight):** "In matters of indifference it was recommended that the Gentile believers should abstain from those things that might hinder the preaching of the gospel and offend weaker brethren." He adds: "Certainly fornication is not a matter of indifference… Yet, it was treated as a matter of indifference because to the Gentiles, who were uninstructed in the law of God, it was commonly looked upon as such." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fdc/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Grant (StudyLight):** These were not merely Jewish laws but "basic in creation from the beginning" — pollutions of idols insults God's place, fornication violates God's established relationships, and eating blood despises God as the life-giver. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/acts-15.html) (excerpt from search results)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The things forbidden are all practices not looked upon as sins by Gentiles, but now enjoined upon them as portions of the Law of Moses which were to be binding upon them, at least for a time, with a view to their living in communion and fellowship with their Jewish brethren. The necessity for some of the prohibitions would cease when the condition of the Church as regards Jews and Gentiles was altered; others were of eternal obligation." [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/acts/15.htm) (excerpt from search results)

---

## Protestant Traditions: Points of Difference

Given what the searched sources reveal, the main differences among Protestant traditions on this passage are not dramatic — all affirm salvation by grace through faith alone. However, some nuances emerge:

- **Baptist (MacArthur/GTY, Gill):** Strong emphasis on *sola fide* and *sola gratia*. MacArthur calls the Jerusalem Council the "Magna Carta of the Christian Church" and insists salvation is "by grace alone, through faith alone, plus nothing." Gill emphasises that the yoke Peter speaks of includes the whole moral law — no mere mortal can bear it. [https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1](https://www.gty.org/sermons/1750/is-salvation-by-law-or-grace-part-1) | [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/acts/15.htm)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Guzik shares the same Reformed-evangelical soteriology. The distinctives are more in application — emphasis on the Holy Spirit's work (v. 8: God giving the Spirit as evidence of acceptance) and the Spirit-filled nature of the Council ("it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us," v. 28, though this falls beyond v. 20). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/)

- **Evangelical/Interdenominational (Precept Austin):** Draws heavily on MacArthur, Spurgeon, and other conservative sources. Emphasises the "battle for the integrity of the Gospel" and warns against modern Hebrew Roots movements that parallel the Judaizer error. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-15-commentary)

- **Churches of Christ (Dunagan):** A distinct note appears in Dunagan's commentary on v. 11: "one is not saved by faith only and neither is one saved by grace alone" — salvation requires obedience including baptism. On v. 19 he emphasises that the apostles argued from "approved examples, necessary inferences, and direct commands" — not feelings or culture. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dun/acts-15.html)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott provides rich historical-grammatical background, emphasising the logical coherence of the Judaizer position (circumcision as "everlasting covenant" never formally abrogated). He notes the distinction between positive/ceremonial and moral/permanent obligations of the Law. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/15.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/15.htm) (excerpt from search results)

- **Lutheran, Methodist, Reformed distinctives:** The searched sites (lcms.org, 1517.org, wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com, ligonier.org, monergism.com) did not yield separate detailed verse-by-verse results for this passage within the search limits. However, the general Protestant consensus represented by the above sources aligns with the Lutheran and Reformed confessions on justification by faith alone.

## Other Views

- **Catholic and Orthodox:** The searched Catholic/Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) did not return specific verse-by-verse results within the search limits. The Catholic tradition generally reads this passage as affirming that the Mosaic ceremonial law is not binding on Gentile Christians, while still recognising the Council of Jerusalem as a model for the Church's Magisterium (the apostles and elders acting as a teaching authority issuing binding decrees). The Orthodox tradition sees this Council (Acts 15) as the prototype of the Ecumenical Councils.

- **Modern Scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey):** Not accessed within tool limits. The NET Bible notes are known to discuss the textual variants in Amos 9:11-12 (LXX vs. MT) that James quotes — the LXX reads "the remnant of men may seek the Lord" while the MT reads "they may possess the remnant of Edom," a significant difference in how James applies the prophecy.

- **Modern debated teachings:** Not specifically sourced within limits. Hyper-grace teachers might use vv. 10-11 (the law as an unbearable yoke; salvation by grace) to argue against any ongoing role for moral law in the believer's life. The traditional response, as seen in the commentaries above, is that the four restrictions in v. 20 show that grace does not mean lawlessness — some moral requirements (especially sexual immorality) remain binding.
